title: Effectiveness of Verifier‑in‑the‑Loop Generate–Validate–Repair for Natural‑Language → Configuration Translation in Emulated Multi‑Device Networks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory evaluation (N=200 paired multi‑device intents) testing whether a bounded generate–validate–repair pipeline that places a formal verifier in the loop reduces semantic configuration errors versus a single‑pass LLM generation. Execution used containerized FRRouting/VyOS images, Batfish verification, and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Critically, the preregistered design used a shared initial LLM candidate for baseline and guarded conditions (shared_initial_generation), so the guarded pipeline could only differ when a verifier‑guided repair was produced; this choice intentionally controls generation variance but decreases sensitivity to marginal repair gains. All confirmatory pairs completed and both baseline and guarded conditions passed the deterministic validator in every episode (n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The paired absolute success‑rate difference = 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0) and the preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). We therefore do not find a verifier‑measured marginal benefit under these constrained conditions; we (1) give a precise, enumerated validator decision rule tied to archived validator traces, (2) explain how the shared_initial_generation design produced a ceiling (zero discordant pairs) that renders McNemar uninformative for marginal repair detection, (3) report representative task difficulty diagnostics from archived exemplars, and (4) document threats to validity that limit external generalization.

sections.introduction: Generative language models are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks that translate operator intent into device configuration changes. Prior work emphasizes verifier‑grounded, closed‑loop architectures to avoid semantic outages caused by unsafe ordering, reachability violations, or hallucinated commands. We preregistered a paired experiment (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001) to measure the marginal verifier value: does an iterative generate–validate–repair loop using a formal verifier (Batfish) reduce critical semantic errors in LLM‑generated multi‑device configurations relative to a single LLM generation? Our contribution is an artifact‑backed, preregistered paired test that (a) reports exact paired outcomes and statistical inference, (b) states the deterministic validator decision rule used to assign verifier_pass, (c) highlights a key design choice (shared_initial_generation) that trades variance control for detectability and produced a ceiling effect in the confirmatory cohort, and (d) supplies representative difficulty diagnostics from archived exemplars to contextualize the constrained result.
sections.related_work: Surveys and recent benchmark efforts document active research on LLMs and agentic pipelines for NetOps and AIOps and propose verifier‑assisted workflows for reachability and policy checking. Formal verification tools (e.g., Batfish, header‑space engines, SMT‑based verifiers) are standard validators for many semantic properties. Empirical benchmarks show that LLM outputs can fail on syntax, ordering, and semantic constraints, motivating generate–validate–repair designs; however, prior studies vary in model sets, task realism, and validator integration, leaving unresolved how much marginal safety verifiers add in controlled, preregistered paired tests. Our work situates a preregistered paired test within this literature by measuring the guarded pipeline's marginal effect in a single‑model, emulation‑grounded regime.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and sampling. We preregistered CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 and froze sampling, analysis, timeouts, retry, and inclusion/exclusion rules prior to execution. Confirmatory sampling: N=200 multi‑device intents stratified into three topology clusters: (A) 2 devices: 80 intents; (B) 3–4 devices: 80 intents; (C) 5–8 devices: 40 intents. Model and generation. The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini and the preregistered execution used a single shared initial generation per intent (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate; independent_condition_generation = false). The guarded pipeline allowed at most one verifier‑guided repair iteration per intent. Validator and pass rule. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) combines three ordered checks and assigns a binary verifier_pass when the post‑validation state passes all checks. Concretely: (1) Parsing/normalization: canonicalize generated command sequence into normalized lines and extract parsed command objects; count parsed vs required commands. (2) Task‑payload constraints: check required‑sequence presence and preserved‑state constraints by comparing the normalized final configuration to the task's expected_final_state and by asserting presence/ordering of required commands encoded in the task payload. (3) Formal reachability/policy checks: run Batfish on the emulated topology and translate any reachability/policy counterexamples into violation codes. The validator deterministically assigns verifier_pass when validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 in the archived validator_trace for an episode (see representative validator_trace files in the artifact bundle under execution/scoring/ and execution/responses/). This boolean rule is the operative outcome used in the paired test. Execution environment and logging. Execution used containerized Mininet‑style emulation with FRRouting and VyOS images, Batfish as the verifier, and deterministic task generation. Timeouts, retries, missingness and multiplicity rules followed the preregistration. All raw model responses, validator traces, and run logs were archived; representative examples include execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (see artifact bundle). Statistical analysis. The preregistered primary test is an exact two‑sided McNemar test on paired binary semantic‑error outcomes (alpha=0.05). The primary estimand is the absolute paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) with a 95% bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10000). The preregistration also specified sensitivity and subgroup analyses; those are discussed as appropriate given the confirmatory outcome.
sections.results: Execution and paired outcomes. Execution completed per plan: 400 episodes (200 baseline + 200 guarded) and zero failed episodes. The archived paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline_success_count = 200; guarded_success_count = 200. The exact McNemar two‑sided test returns p = 1.0. The paired absolute success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) estimate = 0.00 with a 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10000). Cause of the null result. No repair attempts were applied for confirmatory episodes because the shared_initial_candidate satisfied the deterministic validator for every episode (validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0). Thus the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to change outcomes in the confirmatory cohort. Representative difficulty diagnostics. Representative statistics from six archived exemplars included in the artifact bundle show changed_interface_count = {1,2,2,2,2,2} (mean = 1.83, median = 2); required_command_count = {4,2,6,4,3,6} (mean = 4.17, median = 4); dependency_rule_count commonly = 2; difficulty labels include medium/hard/very_hard. Contamination and exclusions. The preregistered contamination filters flagged zero exact‑hash duplicates and no high n‑gram overlap within the confirmatory N; no confirmatory episodes were excluded. Explorer reserve. The confirmatory run completed as planned and the preregistered exploratory reserve was not executed for the confirmatory cohort.
sections.discussion: Statistical interpretation and detectability. McNemar's test is uninformative when there are zero discordant pairs: the observed contingency (n10 = n01 = 0) yields p = 1.0 but provides no evidence about potential marginal improvements that could occur under different generation semantics. The degenerate 95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00] arises because all paired differences are zero; bootstrap resampling of identical paired outcomes reproduces zero differences, producing a zero‑width percentile interval. These observations are consequences of the preregistered shared_initial_generation design, which intentionally controls generation variance by using the same initial LLM candidate for both conditions. That design reduces confounding from LLM randomness but at the cost of sensitivity to marginal repair effects when the initial candidate already passes validator checks; this tradeoff must be treated as a principal internal‑validity limitation of the confirmatory test. Validator ↔ emulator relationship. In the confirmatory cohort there were no episodes with validator_pass ≠ emulation success: archived validator_trace entries show validation_after.valid == true and violation_count == 0 when the episode was scored as a pass, and execution accounting recorded zero failed episodes. Thus, within these artifacts, validator_pass corresponded to deterministically validated final states produced from emulation‑grounded checks; nonetheless, the deterministic validator does not capture hardware timing/race quirks or some vendor‑specific idiosyncrasies not represented by FRR/VyOS images, limiting construct and external validity. Operational implications and recommendations. The absence of an observed marginal verifier benefit here should not be interpreted as evidence that verifiers are unnecessary. Rather, it illustrates that exposure of marginal repair utility depends on (at least) model diversity, task/adversary selection, emulator fidelity, and experimental generation semantics. For future studies we recommend: (a) independent per‑condition generation or multiple independent generations per intent to increase detectability of repair effects; (b) broader model and vendor image diversity; (c) adversarial/noisy intent sets to surface failure modes; and (d) inclusion of trace‑centered metrics (tool calls, counterexample provenance, rollback correctness) rather than only final binary pass/fail.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired confirmatory evaluation comparing a bounded verifier‑in‑the‑loop generate–validate–repair pipeline vs single‑pass LLM generation for NL→config translation in emulated multi‑device networks, both baseline and guarded conditions passed the deterministic validator for all confirmatory intents (n11 = 200; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The guarded repair stage produced no measurable marginal verifier‑measured benefit under the constrained study conditions (paired difference = 0.00; McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00]). We provide an explicit validator decision rule, explain the preregistered shared_initial_generation detectability tradeoff that produced a ceiling, and present representative difficulty diagnostics from archived exemplars. To assess practical marginal utility of verifier‑guided repair in NetOps, future work must broaden model and device diversity, include adversarial intents and independent generation semantics, and adopt trace‑centered evaluation metrics.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory). The study was executed autonomously from a frozen initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Declared LLM: gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. Orchestration/adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 was frozen before execution (preregistration manifest referenced in execution manifest). Execution components: containerized Mininet‑style emulation using FRRouting and VyOS images; Batfish used as the formal verifier; deterministic task generator; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scoring rule. The validator assigns verifier_pass when the archived validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 in the validator_trace (this combines parsing/normalization, required‑sequence and preserved‑state checks, and Batfish reachability/policy tests as described in Methods). The confirmatory run used a shared initial generation per intent for baseline and guarded conditions (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate), a preregistered design choice that intentionally controls generation variance and is discussed in the manuscript as a detectability tradeoff. All experiment orchestration, model calls, verifications, emulation runs, scoring, logging, and analysis were performed autonomously per the preregistration; humans acted only as Research Director prior to the autonomy lock and to receive final outputs after autonomous completion. Execution completed without technical restarts affecting confirmatory pairs (completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). The artifact bundle includes archived raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts (refer to execution/ and analysis/ paths in the bundle) for machine verification.
limitations: Single model family: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; conclusions do not generalize across models or families.
Device and vendor scope: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only (no proprietary vendor images).
Synthetic task generator: tasks were deterministically generated and may not capture full operator ambiguity, legacy runbook phrasing, or adversarial intent distributions.
Emulator fidelity: containerized Mininet‑style emulation does not fully replicate hardware idiosyncrasies, timing, or race conditions of production devices.

Design detectability tradeoff: shared_initial_generation (shared initial candidate for baseline and guarded) was chosen to control generation variance but reduces sensitivity to detect marginal repair benefits (a principal internal‑validity limitation).
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑pass outputs passed the validator for all confirmatory intents, producing a null marginal effect and limiting exploratory inference.

Contamination uncertainty: deterministic exact‑hash checks found zero matches in confirmatory N and n‑gram overlap detectors reported no high‑overlap flags, but undetected paraphrase overlap with model training data cannot be fully ruled out.
Security scenarios: prompt‑injection, retrieval poisoning, and adversarial telemetry perturbations were not evaluated and remain open threats for agentic NetOps systems.
